These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Identity and context

The Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee identifies its people as Eeyou and locates its homeland primarily in northern Québec, with historically occupied lands in Ontario. Its community account emphasizes distinct local histories alongside shared connections and describes local governments working through regional institutions.

Read the sources [1] Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee) / Cree Nation Government

02

A path for deeper reading

Start with this government's own community descriptions and follow its links to individual First Nations. Research beyond Eeyou Istchee is still needed before this guide can represent the wider range of Cree communities and languages.

Read the sources [1] Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee) / Cree Nation Government

03

A James Bay institution for cultural knowledge

In its own retrospective, Aanischaaukamikw describes decades of discussion leading to a cultural institute at Oujé-Bougoumou. It dates an intensified project to1998, construction to2009 and the first public opening toNovember2011. The account introduces a James Bay Cree effort to preserve and share knowledge; it does not stand for every Cree community or establish the results of all later programs.

Read the sources [2] Aanischaaukamikw Cree Cultural Institute

What needs further research

  • The old Cow Creek Umpqua publication is unrelated to Cree and should be replaced, not relabelled.
  • The source distinguishes local First Nations and an Eeyou regional government; these are not a single government for all Cree people.
  • No census counts, area totals, current officers, present treaty membership or current legal conclusions are asserted.
  • Keep the broader entry name Cree and kind Wider grouping / peoples. This is a limited starter reading path, not a proposed renaming of all Cree as Eeyou.
  • Do not add unrelated Plains Cree, Nêhiyaw or other regional assertions from this one page. No map data or canonical source was edited.
  • Extend reading through independently scoped Cree communities and languages beyond Eeyou Istchee; this path is not a history of all Cree peoples.
  • Inspect original institutional records and public community evaluations before extending the Institute’s retrospective or claiming later outcomes.
  • Add community-directed language, family and historical publications with their own dates and access limits.
  • Keep the existing James Bay Cree hood as one specifically attributed museum object, not every Cree community’s attire or a present-government portrait.
  • No current demographic totals, officeholders, legal powers, program availability or universal community endorsement are established.

History — Aanischaaukamikw Cree Cultural Institute ↗

The Institute’s own retrospective traces planning, institutional partnerships, construction and its2011 public opening. It records a specifically James Bay Cree institution, not every Cree community or a measured account of all later programming.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete substantive History body on the public legacy site, web lines27–34:1998 planning, named architect/site, partnerships,2009 construction and November2011 public opening. The1998 quotation is historical testimony, not a current officeholder statement.
